Model Response:

Corporate Capital Punishment: The Case for Dissolving Corporations That Repeatedly Break the Law

Introduction

In 2012, HSBC paid $1.9 billion to settle charges that it had laundered money for Mexican drug cartels and terrorist organizations. The fine represented roughly five weeks of profit. No executives went to prison. The bank continued operating. In 2015, Volkswagen engineered one of the most brazen frauds in automotive history, deliberately deceiving emissions regulators across the globe. The company paid fines, reshuffled leadership, and today sells millions of cars annually. In 2020, Boeing faced scrutiny for conduct that investigators concluded contributed to 346 deaths across two 737 MAX crashes, with evidence suggesting executives had prioritized speed and profit over safety, then obscured what they knew. Boeing received a deferred prosecution agreement, paid settlements, and continues to manufacture aircraft under government contracts worth billions.

Each of these cases illustrates a structural failure at the heart of corporate accountability: the penalties attached to even catastrophic corporate wrongdoing are routinely insufficient to deter recurrence, because corporations as currently constituted are designed to absorb financial punishment and continue operating. The solution, uncomfortable as it may be, is to treat chronic or egregious corporate criminality the same way we treat individual criminals who demonstrate they cannot function within legal boundaries — removal from society. The corporate death penalty, meaning the court-ordered forced dissolution of corporations found guilty of repeated or sufficiently serious illegal conduct, is not merely a provocative idea. It is a logical, necessary, and proportionate response to a genuine accountability crisis.

The Fundamental Asymmetry of Corporate Accountability

To understand why the corporate death penalty is necessary, one must first understand why existing remedies fail structurally rather than accidentally.

When an individual commits a serious crime repeatedly, society possesses escalating tools of consequence: fines, probation, incarceration, and in extreme cases, permanent removal from circulation. The logic underlying this escalating framework is straightforward — consequences must be severe enough and certain enough to actually deter the behavior, and when an actor proves incorrigible, society retains the authority to protect itself regardless of what that actor prefers.

Corporations, by contrast, operate under a radically asymmetric accountability structure. They can be fined, but fines are simply a cost of doing business when the profit generated by illegal conduct exceeds the expected penalty discounted by the probability of detection. Executives can theoretically be prosecuted individually, but the diffusion of corporate decision-making, the availability of expensive legal insulation, and documented prosecutorial reluctance to pursue individuals — what former Attorney General Eric Holder famously called institutions "too big to jail" — means individual accountability is the exception rather than the rule. Corporations can be placed on probation through deferred prosecution agreements, but these arrangements are negotiated with the very regulators who depend on corporate cooperation, creating well-documented dynamics of leniency. What corporations cannot currently experience — not as a routine legal sanction — is dissolution, the one consequence that would genuinely eliminate the offending entity.

This gap is not incidental. It represents a categorical failure to apply the same logical framework to corporate actors that we apply to individual ones. If a law's purpose is both to punish wrongdoing and deter future conduct, a sanction that leaves the wrongdoer intact and profitable after payment is not a punishment adequate to either purpose. It is a tax.

The Deterrence Argument

The primary justification for any legal sanction is deterrence, and on this criterion, existing corporate penalties have demonstrably failed across multiple industries and across decades.

The financial sector paid over $200 billion in fines and settlements between 2008 and 2018 in connection with frauds, manipulations, and predatory practices surrounding the financial crisis. Within years, the same institutions faced new investigations for rate-fixing, money laundering, and consumer fraud. The pharmaceutical industry has paid billions to settle charges involving illegal marketing of opioids while simultaneously lobbying against regulatory constraints on opioid prescribing. Oil companies have funded systematic disinformation campaigns about climate science while accepting environmental settlements and continuing the same underlying conduct. The pattern across industries is consistent: fines, even large ones, do not deter recurrence when the profit structure of illegal activity remains intact.

This is not surprising. Corporate decision-making is rational in an economic sense, and rational actors respond to incentives. If the expected cost of illegal conduct — the fine multiplied by the probability of being caught, divided by the duration of the scheme — is lower than the expected profit, a corporation staffed with rational profit-maximizers will, on average, commit the illegal conduct. This is not a cynical claim about corporate culture; it is what basic expected utility theory predicts. The only way to fundamentally alter this calculus is to introduce a sanction whose magnitude overwhelms any conceivable benefit. The forced dissolution of a corporation — wiping out shareholder equity, terminating executive compensation, ending the enterprise entirely — is the one sanction that unambiguously does so.

Consider what executives and shareholders actually fear. Fines reduce quarterly profits and may deflate stock prices temporarily. Criminal prosecution of individuals is rare enough to be treated as catastrophic bad luck rather than systemic expectation. But dissolution eliminates everything — the company's value, the executives' platform, the shareholders' investment, the brand that took decades to build. If corporate boards understood that a second major criminal conviction, or a first sufficiently egregious one, meant the enterprise ceased to exist, the board-level risk calculus would change fundamentally. Compliance would become an existential priority rather than a line item.

The Proportionality Argument

Critics of the corporate death penalty frequently invoke harm to innocent parties — employees who would lose jobs, shareholders who committed no crime, communities dependent on the company's economic activity — as arguments against dissolution. This objection, while emotionally compelling, fails to account for the proportionality framework that governs all serious criminal penalties.

When we imprison an individual, we accept that innocent parties suffer. The criminal's children lose a parent. Their spouse loses a partner and perhaps an income. Their community loses a member. We impose these costs on innocent parties because we have determined that the alternative — allowing serious criminals to continue operating freely — imposes greater costs on society as a whole. The same logic applies to corporate dissolution.

The harms produced by unchecked corporate criminality are neither abstract nor small. The opioid epidemic, to which pharmaceutical executives and distributors contributed through documented illegal marketing and distribution practices, has killed over 500,000 Americans since 1999. The 2008 financial crisis, enabled by fraudulent securitization practices and deliberate misrepresentation of risk, cost the U.S. economy an estimated $22 trillion in lost output and wealth. Environmental crimes committed by energy companies have contaminated drinking water, destroyed ecosystems, and produced public health crises affecting millions of people who bear no resemblance to the shareholders who profited. Compared against these documented harms, the disruption produced by dissolving an offending company — distributing its assets, allowing competitors to absorb its labor force and operations, compensating affected workers through structured wind-down processes — is proportionate and defensible.

Moreover, the harm-to-innocents argument applies with greatest force to exactly the kinds of companies where it should carry least moral weight: corporations so large and dominant that their dissolution would significantly disrupt markets. That a corporation has become "too big to punish" without systemic consequence is not an argument for exempting it from meaningful accountability; it is an argument, separately, for preventing corporations from becoming so large that their criminality can be held hostage against the public interest. Accepting the too-big-to-punish logic as a permanent shield is effectively accepting that sufficiently powerful corporations are above the law — a conclusion incompatible with the rule of law itself.

The Structural Design Argument

Beyond deterrence and proportionality, there is a deeper structural argument for the corporate death penalty rooted in the nature of the corporate form itself.

Corporations are not naturally occurring entities. They are legal constructs created by society through legislation and judicial interpretation, granted extraordinary privileges — limited liability, perpetual existence, legal personhood, the ability to accumulate capital across generations — that no human being possesses. These privileges are granted on the implicit and sometimes explicit understanding that corporations will operate within the legal framework society establishes. When a corporation systematically and repeatedly violates that framework, it has broken the foundational compact that justifies the grant of these privileges.

Limited liability, in particular, becomes morally untenable when paired with immunity from dissolution. Limited liability means that shareholders cannot lose more than their investment regardless of the harm the corporation causes. This is an extraordinary protection, one that enables capital formation and economic dynamism at scale. But it also means that shareholders have a structural incentive to tolerate risk-taking and legal boundary-pushing that produces profits for them while externalizing costs onto the public. If the worst outcome shareholders face is a fine that reduces but does not eliminate their returns, the moral hazard is baked into the system. Dissolution is the natural complement to limited liability — the mechanism by which society can say "your investment is forfeit" when the entity you funded has caused sufficient harm through illegal conduct.

This is not unprecedented in legal or regulatory frameworks. State attorneys general in the United States already possess authority to dissolve corporations chartered in their states for conduct "contrary to public policy." The federal government revoked the charter of the Bank of the United States in the 19th century, effectively ending its existence. Arthur Andersen, the accounting firm, was effectively destroyed by its 2002 criminal indictment in connection with the Enron scandal — though the mechanism was indirect, with clients fleeing rather than a court ordering dissolution. The corporate death penalty formalizes and regularizes an authority that already exists in fragmentary form, providing it with procedural integrity that the Arthur Andersen case, where the Supreme Court ultimately overturned the conviction after the firm had already ceased to exist, demonstrably lacked.

Addressing the Serious Objections

Intellectually honest advocacy requires engaging with the strongest counterarguments rather than dismissing them.

The systemic risk objection holds that dissolving large corporations could destabilize financial markets or critical industries. This is a legitimate concern that demands procedural rather than substantive concession. A well-designed corporate death penalty statute would include graduated timelines for wind-down, mechanisms for orderly transfer of operations and assets, protections for workers including severance and retraining obligations funded from corporate assets prior to distribution, and judicial discretion to impose dissolution prospectively rather than immediately. The goal is elimination of the offending entity, not economic chaos. Regulatory frameworks for bank resolution already demonstrate that large financial institutions can be wound down in orderly ways when the political will exists to do so.

The chilling effect objection holds that fear of dissolution would paralyze corporate risk-taking and innovation. This objection conflates illegal risk and legal risk, a distinction that should not be blurred in public policy. Corporations should be chilled from taking illegal risks — that is precisely the point. There is no legitimate argument that the prospect of corporate dissolution should deter legal business activity, any more than the prospect of imprisonment deters law-abiding individuals from living their lives. If corporate counsel cannot distinguish between aggressive-but-legal business conduct and criminal behavior, the problem lies with corporate counsel rather than with the existence of a meaningful penalty.

The innocent shareholders objection has been partially addressed above, but deserves additional engagement. Shareholders are not uniformly innocent. Institutional investors, activist shareholders, and boards bear responsibility for the governance cultures they create and tolerate. More importantly, the shareholder loss produced by dissolution is qualitatively different from punishment of innocents — it is the elimination of an investment whose value was partly generated by illegal conduct. The investor who profited, even unknowingly, from illegal activity that harmed others has a weaker claim to restitution than intuition suggests. A structured wind-down that prioritizes employee protections and victim compensation over shareholder recovery reflects appropriate moral ordering.

The prosecutorial abuse objection holds that dissolution authority would be weaponized by politically motivated prosecutors against disfavored companies. This is a genuine institutional risk that demands robust procedural safeguards: independent judicial approval, high evidentiary standards, appellate review, clear statutory definitions of qualifying conduct, and potentially a specialized corporate accountability court insulated from direct political pressure. These are design questions, not arguments against the principle. The same objection could be made against virtually any powerful legal tool; the answer is careful institutional design, not abandonment of the tool.

Toward a Framework

A serious corporate death penalty statute would need to define its triggers carefully. Reasonable criteria might include: conviction on felony charges for a third offense within a defined period; a first conviction where the criminal conduct caused death or serious physical injury to ten or more persons and executive knowledge is demonstrated; or a first conviction for conduct specifically designed to defeat regulatory oversight — fraud upon a regulator, systematic evidence destruction, deliberate maintenance of a criminal enterprise at the executive level. The statute should establish graduated penalties short of dissolution — enhanced monitoring, government-appointed compliance officers, partial asset divestiture — that serve as escalating warnings before the terminal sanction. Dissolution itself should require judicial approval at multiple stages, with full adversarial process and appellate rights intact.

Critically, the corporate death penalty should be understood as complementary to, not a replacement for, robust individual prosecution. The lesson of recent decades is that fines without individual accountability produced neither deterrence nor justice. A complete corporate accountability framework includes aggressive prosecution of the executives who authorized or enabled criminal conduct, civil liability for affected parties, and — at the extreme end of recidivism and severity — dissolution of the entity itself.

Conclusion

The corporate death penalty is not a radical proposition. It is the logical extension of principles that already govern every other domain of legal accountability: that consequences must be sufficient to actually deter conduct, that recidivists face escalating sanctions, and that entities granted extraordinary legal privileges bear extraordinary obligations to operate within the law. The current framework, where the worst realistic outcome facing a criminally convicted corporation is a negotiated fine that reduces but doesn't eliminate profitability, has produced decades of recidivism across industries and a growing public conviction — well-supported by evidence — that large corporations operate under a different set of rules than ordinary citizens.

If we believe that no individual is above the law, we must accept the corollary that no corporation is either. The corporate death penalty is the mechanism that makes that principle something other than rhetoric. Its absence is not a moderate, cautious position — it is a choice, made repeatedly and explicitly, to exempt the most consequential economic actors in modern society from the accountability standards applied to everyone else. That choice has victims. They are identifiable. And the case for changing course has never been stronger.

The Case for a Corporate Death Penalty: Dismantling Impunity Through Forced Dissolution

Corporations are artificial entities granted extraordinary privileges by the state: limited liability that shields owners and executives from personal financial ruin, perpetual existence beyond individual lifespans, and the ability to amass resources rivaling those of nations. In exchange, they are expected to operate within the bounds of law. When they repeatedly or egregiously violate those bounds—through fraud, environmental devastation, labor exploitation, or systemic corruption—the current regime of fines, settlements, and occasional executive prosecutions has proven woefully inadequate. A corporate death penalty, enforced as the forced dissolution and winding-down of such entities, is not radical punishment; it is the logical correction to restore genuine accountability and deter misconduct at the institutional level.

The central failure of existing enforcement is that corporations treat legal violations as a routine cost of doing business. Multi-billion-dollar fines, such as those imposed on financial institutions following the 2008 crisis or pharmaceutical companies for opioid-related wrongdoing, are frequently absorbed without existential threat. Executives depart with golden parachutes; shareholders see temporary stock dips followed by recovery; and the corporation rebrands, restructures minimally, or simply pays the fine while continuing operations. This dynamic creates a moral hazard: conduct that would destroy a human offender's life or freedom is reduced to an actuarial calculation. For evidence, consider the repeated recidivism of major banks implicated in money laundering, LIBOR manipulation, and foreclosure abuses. If dissolution had been the default remedy after the second or third major offense, the incentive structure would invert—compliance would become survival-critical rather than optional.

Limited liability, a foundational corporate privilege, loses its justification when companies systematically externalize harm onto society. Investors and managers enjoy protection from downside risks precisely because society presumes responsible behavior backed by state enforcement power. When that presumption collapses under patterns of willful illegality, dissolution functions as clawback: the entity dissolves, assets are liquidated under court supervision, creditors are addressed according to priority, and any remaining value flows to victims or the public fisc. This approach aligns corporate incentives with those imposed on individuals. A repeat-offender sole proprietor faces bankruptcy or license revocation; an equivalent corporation should face equivalent existential consequence rather than perpetual reincarnation through subsidiaries, mergers, or name changes.

Critics often contend that dissolution would destroy jobs, disrupt supply chains, and punish innocent employees and shareholders. These objections, while superficially compelling, ignore the alternatives already in operation and the data from analogous enforcement tools. High-profile bankruptcies and divestitures routinely occur in markets without triggering systemic collapse; orderly wind-downs, as seen in certain bank resolutions during crises, have preserved critical functions through transfers to compliant buyers. Employees and suppliers can migrate or be absorbed. Shareholders, having chosen to invest in a law-breaking enterprise, bear the market risk they already accept. Most importantly, the absence of dissolution imposes diffuse costs on society: poisoned water tables from corporate pollution, foreclosed homes from fraudulent lending, or eroded public trust from health scandals affect far broader populations than any single firm's payroll. Prioritizing the "too big to dissolve" argument perpetuates a two-tiered justice system where size confers de facto immunity.

The deterrent value extends beyond the individual firm. Markets price in the realistic probability of severe penalty. If repeated violations carried dissolution risk, due diligence by investors, insurers, and board members would intensify preemptively. Compliance departments would gain genuine authority rather than serving as window-dressing. Historical precedents exist in other domains: professional license revocation for lawyers or doctors, charter revocation for charities, or nationalization/expropriation in cases of egregious state-corporate collusion. Extending this logic to private corporations is consistent with the principle that no entity possesses rights without corresponding duties.

Implementation requires careful legal design to prevent abuse: thresholds tied to repeated adjudicated violations over a defined period, clear definitions of "egregious" conduct involving harm to life, widespread fraud, or environmental catastrophe, and provisions for successor liability to block shell recreations. Federal legislation could amend corporate charters and securities law to make dissolution a statutory remedy available to regulators or private plaintiffs after exhaustion of lesser sanctions. Such reforms would not eliminate all corporate power—compliant entities would continue operating—but they would remove the safety net that currently rewards serial lawbreaking.

Corporations exist at society's sufferance. When they repeatedly demonstrate that their internal governance structures prioritize illicit gain over legal compliance, society retains both the right and the practical necessity to withdraw that existence. Fines and individual prosecutions have not sufficed; incremental reform has not sufficed. A corporate death penalty would reassert that legal personhood is revocable, restoring the balance between privilege and responsibility that the corporate form was always intended to maintain.

The Corporate Death Penalty: A Necessary Mechanism for True Accountability

In the landscape of modern capitalism, we have crafted a disturbing paradox. We grant corporations many of the legal rights of individuals—the right to free speech, the right to lobby governments, the right to amass wealth—yet we consistently balk at holding them to the same standard of accountability when their actions cause catastrophic harm. When an individual repeatedly commits serious crimes, society has mechanisms to permanently remove them from the community. Yet when a corporation does the same—poisoning water supplies, engineering deadly product defects, or orchestrating systemic fraud—the typical penalty is a fine, often representing a fraction of the ill-gotten gains. This imbalance is not just unjust; it is dangerous. To rectify this, we must formally implement and regularly utilize a "corporate death penalty": the forced dissolution of corporations found guilty of repeated or egregious illegal behavior.

The current system of corporate accountability is fundamentally broken. Fines, the predominant penalty, have proven woefully inadequate as a deterrent. For large multinational corporations, these financial sanctions are merely a "cost of doing business," a line item budgeted for and factored into profit calculations. When the penalty for illegally dumping toxic waste is a $10 million fine against $500 million in profits from the illegal activity, the rational economic choice is to continue the misconduct. This creates a perverse incentive structure where illegal behavior is financially rewarded. The corporate death penalty would change this calculus entirely. The threat of total organizational extinction would compel boards, executives, and shareholders to implement rigorous, proactive compliance systems. It would make ethical behavior not just a moral choice, but an existential necessity for the organization's survival.

Historically, our legal system has recognized that certain privileges can be forfeited through misconduct. A lawyer who repeatedly defrauds clients is disbarred. A doctor who causes willful harm loses their medical license. A charter school that fails students chronically can have its charter revoked. We understand that when an entity entrusted with societal responsibility proves itself irredeemably harmful, its right to operate must be terminated. Corporations are chartered by the state and granted extraordinary privileges—limited liability, perpetual life, personhood. It is a profound societal contract. When a corporation systematically violates that contract, engaging in conduct that shows a willful disregard for law and human welfare, society has not only the right but the moral obligation to revoke its charter and dissolve the entity.

The argument against dissolution often centers on the harm to innocent stakeholders—employees, local communities, and ethical shareholders. This concern, while valid, is ultimately a red herring. First, the harm already exists. A corporation engaging in repeated egregious misconduct is already harming its employees (who face ethical crises and job insecurity from inevitable scandal), its communities (which bear the brunt of pollution, fraud, or unsafe products), and its ethical shareholders (whose investment is devalued by the misconduct). Dissolution, when properly structured, can actually mitigate this harm through orderly wind-downs, asset sales to more responsible entities, and employee transitions. Moreover, the threat of dissolution would incentivize shareholders and boards to police their own companies far more vigorously, creating internal checks long before external dissolution becomes necessary.

Implementation need not be chaotic. A graduated system could be established: corporations with repeated serious violations could be placed on a "corporate probation," subject to intense oversight. Only those that demonstrate a pattern of willful, systemic, and harmful illegality—one that survives changes in leadership and persists despite repeated sanctions—would face the final step of dissolution. Essential services could be maintained through temporary public stewardship or mandated sale to a responsible buyer. The key principle is that no entity, no matter how large or economically important, should be considered "too big to fail" when it becomes too corrupt to survive.

Ultimately, the corporate death penalty is about restoring the foundational principle of justice: that with great power comes great responsibility. For decades, we have allowed corporations to accumulate unprecedented power while diluting their accountability to meaningless fines. This has contributed to a crisis of public trust in capitalism itself. By implementing a mechanism for corporate dissolution in cases of egregious misconduct, we send an unequivocal message: corporations exist at the pleasure of society, and when they betray that trust in fundamental ways, they will cease to exist. This is not anti-corporate sentiment; it is pro-accountability, pro-responsibility, and ultimately, pro-ethical capitalism. The corporate death penalty doesn't threaten the free market; it saves it from its own worst actors, clearing the ground for businesses that respect both law and humanity to thrive.

Adopting a "corporate death penalty" policy—forcing the dissolution of corporations engaged in serious or repeated illegal acts—is a concept debated in legal and economic theory. Here are the key reasons and supposed benefits often cited by proponents, presented factually and neutrally:

  • Extension of Legal Personhood:
    In many jurisdictions, corporations are treated as legal persons.   • Systemic Risk Mitigation:
    For corporations that repeatedly engage in harmful acts (e.g., banks involved in systemic financial fraud, polluters causing ecological damage), dissolution could remove a persistent source of risk to the public, the economy, or the environment.

  • Moral and Symbolic Accountability:

2. Supposed Benefits

  • Behavioral Change:
    Beyond fines, which may be perceived as manageable expenses, dissolution threats could fundamentally alter corporate behavior, encouraging investment in compliance and ethical governance.

  • Market Correction:
    Removing chronically harmful corporations could allow market share to shift to more responsible competitors, potentially raising industry standards.

  • Public Trust Restoration:
    In cases of severe or repeated misconduct, dissolution might help restore public trust in regulatory systems and the business environment.

  • Addressing "Too Big to Jail" Critiques:
    Proponents suggest it could overcome the difficulty of prosecuting large corporations, where criminal charges might threaten jobs or economic stability, by offering a structured, legal process for dissolution.

3. Criticisms and Practical Challenges

  • Economic Collateral Damage:
    Dissolution could lead to massive job losses, disrupt supply chains, harm innocent shareholders (including pension funds), and impact communities dependent on the corporation.

  • Implementation Complexity:
    Determining thresholds for "serious or repeated" illegal acts, managing asset liquidation, and ensuring due process are significant legal and administrative challenges.

4. Current Legal Precedents

  • In some jurisdictions, courts already have the power to dissolve corporations for misconduct (e.g., "corporate death penalty" provisions in certain U.S. states for fraud). However, these are rarely used.
  • Regulatory approaches more commonly emphasize fines, sanctions, monitoring, and structural reforms rather than outright dissolution.

Conclusion

The corporate death penalty is a theoretical extension of punitive legal principles to corporate entities, aiming to deter severe misconduct through existential consequences. While proponents highlight its potential to enforce accountability and systemic change, critics raise substantial concerns about economic harm, practicality, and proportionality. The debate often centers on balancing accountability with broader social and economic stability.

The Corporate Death Penalty: A Speech for Accountability

Citizens, lawmakers, and advocates for justice — I stand before you today to speak about a principle that should not be controversial: no entity, regardless of its size, its wealth, or its political connections, should be above the law.

That charter is a privilege, not a birthright. It comes with conditions. Among those conditions is the expectation that the corporation will operate within the bounds of the law.

When a company repeatedly, systematically, and knowingly breaks the law — when it poisons communities, defrauds consumers, corrupts institutions, or exploits its workers — the question is not whether we can revoke that charter. The question is: why don't we?

We already have this authority. Every jurisdiction in the world grants the power to revoke the legal existence of a corporation. But this power sits in a drawer, gathering dust, while the public pays the price.

The Cost of Inaction

Let me tell you what happens when we fail to use this power.

We create a system where fines become a cost of doing business — where the penalty for breaking the law is simply another line item in a quarterly budget. When a corporation calculates that the profit from illegal conduct exceeds the fine it will pay, it has a financial incentive to break the law. We have built a system that rewards criminality.

Consider the corporations that have been fined billions of dollars — billions — for actions that destroyed lives. They polluted rivers. They marketed addictive substances they knew were killing people. They manipulated markets that families depended on for their retirement. And after the fine? After the settlement? They kept operating. They kept growing. The executives who made the decisions kept their bonuses.

Where is the justice in that?

A young person caught with a small quantity of drugs may lose their freedom for years. A corporation that floods entire communities with addictive, lethal substances pays a fine and moves on. That is not accountability. That is not justice. That is a system with two sets of rules — one for the powerful, and one for everyone else.

Now, I know the objections. I have heard them. Let me address them honestly.

"But what about the workers?"

This is a serious concern, and it deserves a serious answer. When we shut down a factory that is poisoning a town, do we keep it open to protect the jobs? No — we shut it down and invest in the community's recovery. The same principle applies here. A corporation facing dissolution can be required to establish worker transition funds, retraining programs, and severance obligations as conditions of the proceedings. Assets can be transferred. Essential services can be maintained. But the idea that we must allow a criminal enterprise to continue operating indefinitely because it employs people is an argument for never holding any large employer accountable for anything. That is not a principled position — it is surrender.

No. Criminal behavior destabilizes the economy. Accountability stabilizes it. If corporations know that repeated, egregious violations carry existential consequences — not just fines, but the revocation of their right to exist — behavior will change. Compliance will become a genuine priority, not a public relations exercise. Markets function best when rules are enforced. A market without accountability is not a free market — it is a jungle.

I am not calling for the dissolution of every company that makes a mistake. I am calling for a proportional, judicial process — one that is triggered by repeated, egregious, willful violations of the law. A process with due process. With evidence. With the right to appeal. With independent oversight.

But I am also calling for a system where the most powerful actors in our society face consequences that are proportional to the harm they cause. A system where the law is not a suggestion. Where a corporate charter is not a shield against justice. Where accountability is not a word we use in speeches and then forget when the lobbyists arrive.

The Case for a Corporate Death Penalty: Holding Corporations Accountable

In recent decades, corporate misconduct has reached alarming levels, with scandals involving fraud, environmental destruction, labor exploitation, and even mass harm to consumers. Yet, despite fines and settlements, many corporations continue to engage in illegal and unethical behavior because the consequences are often little more than a slap on the wrist. To truly deter corporate crime and ensure justice, society must implement a corporate death penalty—the forced dissolution of companies that repeatedly or egregiously violate the law. This measure is not only justified but necessary to restore accountability, protect the public, and prevent future harm.

The Failures of Current Corporate Accountability

Today, corporations that break the law typically face financial penalties, deferred prosecutions, or symbolic reforms—none of which fundamentally alter their behavior. For example:

  • Wells Fargo was fined $3 billion in 2020 for systematically defrauding customers, yet the bank continued operating as usual. The fine, while large, was a fraction of its profits, and no executives faced serious personal consequences.
  • Purdue Pharma, the company behind the opioid crisis, filed for bankruptcy to shield itself from lawsuits, while the Sackler family (its owners) walked away with billions.
  • Boeing has faced multiple scandals, including two fatal 737 MAX crashes, yet remains in business despite evidence of reckless negligence and cover-ups.

These cases demonstrate that fines and settlements do not deter misconduct when they are treated as a cost of doing business rather than an existential threat. If a corporation knows it can break the law, pay a fine, and continue operating, there is no real incentive to change.

Why a Corporate Death Penalty Works

A corporate death penalty—revoking a company’s legal charter and dissolving it entirely—would create real consequences for illegal behavior. This approach has historical and legal precedent:

  1. It Has Been Done Before

    • In 2002, Arthur Andersen, once a major accounting firm, was convicted of obstruction of justice in the Enron scandal and lost its license to practice. While the conviction was later overturned, the firm collapsed due to the loss of public trust and legal standing. This shows that dissolution can work as a deterrent.
    • In 2019, OxyContin manufacturer Purdue Pharma was effectively dissolved in bankruptcy as part of a settlement, though critics argue the penalties were still too lenient for the harm caused.

  2. It Removes the Ability to Repeat Offenses

    • Unlike fines, which corporations can absorb, dissolution prevents future harm by eliminating the entity responsible. A company that has repeatedly endangered lives, defrauded customers, or poisoned the environment has demonstrated it cannot be trusted to operate responsibly.
    • For example, if ExxonMobil were found to have knowingly lied about climate change for decades, a fine would not undo the damage—but shutting it down would prevent further deception and environmental destruction.

  3. It Shifts the Burden of Proof Where It Belongs

    • Currently, regulators and prosecutors face enormous pressure to prove intent in corporate crimes, leading to weak settlements. A corporate death penalty would automatically apply after a certain number of serious violations, removing the need for endless legal battles.
    • This would also discourage corporate recidivism, as companies would know that three strikes means elimination.

  4. It Protects Workers, Consumers, and the Public

    • Many corporate crimes—toxic pollution, unsafe working conditions, financial fraud—directly harm people. Allowing these companies to continue operating normalizes impunity.
    • If a food company knowingly sells contaminated products, or a pharmaceutical giant hides deadly side effects, the public deserves more than an apology and a fine—they deserve permanent protection from that entity.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Opponents of a corporate death penalty often raise the following concerns:

1. "It Would Hurt Innocent Workers and Shareholders"

  • Rebuttal: While dissolution would disrupt employment, the alternative—allowing criminal behavior to continue—harms far more people. Workers can be protected through transition programs, severance, and union support, whereas victims of corporate crimes (e.g., asbestos poisonings, financial fraud) often receive no real justice.
  • Additionally, shareholders bear risk in any business—if they profit from a company’s successes, they must also accept the consequences of its failures.

2. "It Would Discourage Economic Growth"

  • Rebuttal: Unchecked corporate crime already distorts markets by rewarding unethical behavior. If a company only stays profitable by breaking the law, its dissolution corrects market failure rather than harming the economy.
  • Moreover, ethical businesses would benefit from a level playing field where lawbreaking companies cannot undercut them.

3. "Regulators Would Abuse the Power"

  • Rebuttal: Safeguards can be implemented, such as:
    • Clear legal thresholds (e.g., three felony convictions in ten years, or a single case causing mass harm).
    • Judicial oversight to prevent politically motivated dissolutions.
    • Appeals processes to ensure fairness.
  • The current system already allows regulators to impose fines and restrictions—dissolution is simply a stronger, more proportional response to the worst offenses.

4. "Corporations Are Too Big to Fail"

  • Rebuttal: The "too big to fail" argument is a moral hazard—it suggests that certain companies are above the law because of their economic impact. This is unacceptable in a just society.
  • If a corporation is systemically important, it should be broken up or nationalized (as was done with banks during the 2008 crisis) rather than allowed to operate with impunity.

Conclusion: Justice Demands Real Consequences

The current system of fines, warnings, and deferred prosecutions has failed to curb corporate misconduct because it does not impose real consequences. A corporate death penalty would restore accountability, deter future crimes, and protect the public from repeat offenders. While dissolution is a severe measure, it is necessary when corporations demonstrate a pattern of lawlessness that endangers lives, destroys the environment, or undermines democracy.

Society must reject the idea that corporations are untouchable. If a person commits multiple serious crimes, they face imprisonment. If a corporation does the same, it should face permanent shutdown. Only then will we see real corporate responsibility—not just empty apologies and paid settlements, but justice.

If a company commits crimes so serious or persistent that it demonstrates an institutional contempt for the law, society should not be required to preserve it. The question is not whether every violation deserves dissolution. Most do not. Corporate misconduct frequently persists not because corporations are unaware of illegality, but because enforcement outcomes are insufficiently consequential. Consider how corporate wrongdoing typically plays out: regulators impose penalties, corporations pay settlements, and executives often face limited or no personal consequences. Meanwhile, the company continues operating, keeps market share, and—crucially—keeps benefiting from its conduct.

Fines and settlements can be absorbed as costs. Sophisticated entities may estimate expected enforcement risk the same way they estimate expected return on investment. If the “expected penalty” is smaller than the profit from unlawful conduct (including time saved, competitive advantage gained, and liabilities delayed), deterrence collapses. A system that allows corporations to violate laws so long as the financial harm is below the cost threshold does not deter; it optimizes.

A corporate death penalty directly addresses this problem by making certain forms of wrongdoing incompatible with continued existence. If corporations understand that repeated or extreme violations can end the organization, the “cost” equation changes fundamentally.

2. The corporate death penalty targets an ethical and practical core: harm with impunity

When egregious corporate crime is handled with remedies that preserve the same corporate structure, the law sends a message that wrongdoing is survivable. That is ethically corrosive. Corporate harms—fraud that ruins investors, pollution that damages communities, unsafe products that injure or kill—are not abstract. They have victims with real losses and real consequences. Allowing the same entity to remain after catastrophic harm risks turning justice into a transaction rather than a reckoning.

Dissolution in the most serious cases reflects a basic principle: some misconduct demonstrates that an entity cannot be trusted to continue functioning in a role that affects public life. If a corporation repeatedly violates fundamental legal obligations—consumer protection, environmental safety, anti-fraud rules, labor rights, or sanctions compliance—then continuing the entity’s operations amounts to granting it ongoing license to operate despite repeated proof of untrustworthiness.

3. Deterrence requires remedies that meaningfully alter incentives, not symbolic consequences

Deterrence operates under one simple logic: if the expected cost of wrongdoing is low relative to expected benefit, misconduct will continue. Traditional remedies—civil fines, consent decrees, monitoring—often rely on the assumption that internal compliance systems will improve. Yet repeated violations indicate those systems were inadequate or disregarded.

A death penalty is not symbolic. It removes the asset at the center of future profits. It forces boards, shareholders, employees, and lenders to internalize the risk of catastrophic legal outcomes rather than dispersing it across “the business as usual.” This shifts corporate behavior toward rigorous compliance because the downside is existential.

Moreover, the corporate form is uniquely suited to risk-shifting. Corporations can externalize costs onto victims and communities because limited liability caps personal exposure for many stakeholders. A death penalty narrows that gap: the corporate shell cannot repeatedly offload harm and remain intact.

4. It would incentivize responsible governance and discourage “profit at any cost” cultures

A major reason corporate misconduct persists is that internal governance often prioritizes short-term performance. When consequences are limited, boards can treat compliance as a checkbox and allocate resources only when threatened by enforcement. But if dissolution becomes a plausible outcome for repeated or egregious criminal behavior, governance changes.

Boards will demand stronger oversight, real compliance budgets, whistleblower protections, and ethical leadership because they will face existential consequences for failing to prevent—or at least meaningfully mitigate—serious wrongdoing. Employees and managers will also face clearer boundaries: misconduct is not merely a disciplinary issue; it can terminate the company and devastate livelihoods. Public confidence in law depends on the belief that serious wrongdoing leads to serious consequences. That perception fuels cynicism and undermines compliance across sectors.

A corporate death penalty would signal that legal prohibitions are real and enforceable. It would restore credibility for regulators, courts, and victims. Credibility matters: once the public believes enforcement is consequential, companies are more likely to invest in prevention and less likely to gamble on noncompliance.

A frequent objection is that dissolution is too extreme. That concern is legitimate; therefore, any corporate death penalty regime must include stringent safeguards. It should be reserved for clearly defined categories, such as:

  • repeated convictions or proven misconduct after prior enforcement actions,
  • egregious violations with demonstrable harm (or severe risk) to health, safety, or the environment,
  • fraudulent conduct involving systemic deception or deliberate concealment,
  • obstruction of investigations or retaliation against whistleblowers.

Procedurally, death-penalty remedies should require:

  • a high evidentiary standard (e.g., proof beyond a reasonable doubt for criminal convictions, or an equally rigorous standard for structured adjudication),
  • judicial findings that misconduct is systemic and not isolated,
  • consideration of internal compliance failures and whether the company took meaningful corrective action,
  • an opportunity for the company to present evidence of remediation and responsible reforms where applicable,
  • transparency and appellate review.

With such guardrails, dissolution becomes a targeted, principled remedy rather than arbitrary punishment.

Further, dissolution does not have to mean leaving victims without relief. The remedy can be designed to prioritize restitution and compensation:

  • assets can be liquidated to fund victim compensation and environmental remediation,
  • liabilities can be enforced against responsible individuals where evidence exists,
  • successors and related entities can be targeted when laws prevent evasion through restructuring.

In other words, dissolution can be combined with robust victim-centered remedies rather than functioning as a hollow symbolic act.

8. The rule of law should not reward restructuring as a way to escape consequences

Corporate wrongdoing often continues through rebranding, mergers, and shell restructuring. Without a firm “can’t simply reorganize your way out” principle, dissolution loses deterrent power.   • penalties for fraudulently transferring assets to avoid liability,
  • scrutiny of successor liability when misconduct patterns persist.

This ensures that a corporate death penalty is not just a one-time event that can be nullified by legal maneuvering.

When corporations can treat fines as costs, settlements as nuisances, and compliance promises as public relations, accountability becomes performative rather than effective. Dissolving corporations that commit repeated or egregious illegal conduct changes the incentives at the root of corporate behavior. It signals that some wrongdoing is incompatible with continued operation, strengthens deterrence, improves governance, and restores public trust.

The law can and should implement this remedy with strict due process safeguards, clear thresholds, and an emphasis on restitution and enforcement against responsible individuals. The central case for a corporate death penalty is simple: fines often fail. Large corporations can absorb even enormous financial penalties, distribute the pain across shareholders, raise prices, cut worker compensation, or wait for public outrage to fade. Executives may resign with severance packages, and the institution itself survives to offend again. In many cases, the legal system punishes the abstract entity financially without fundamentally changing the incentives, structures, and culture that produced the misconduct. If an organization repeatedly breaks the law because lawbreaking is profitable, then penalties that leave the organization intact may do little more than validate the business model. Dissolution changes that calculus. It communicates that participation in the marketplace is conditional, not absolute, and that corporations exist by public permission, not natural right.

This point is especially important because corporations are legal creations. They are not persons in the biological or moral sense; they are state-chartered entities granted extraordinary privileges, including limited liability, perpetual existence, and access to capital aggregation on a massive scale. These privileges are justified only insofar as corporations serve lawful and socially productive ends. If a corporation repeatedly uses those privileges to commit serious harms, it has violated the terms of its social charter. Forced dissolution is not some radical attack on freedom; it is the revocation of a legal privilege that has been abused. A business that persistently operates as a criminal enterprise should lose the right to exist.

A corporate death penalty would also produce stronger deterrence than current enforcement tools. The most effective deterrent is not merely the possibility of a manageable loss, but the possibility of institutional extinction. Boards of directors, major investors, and top executives would have a far greater incentive to invest in compliance, internal controls, whistleblower protections, and ethical leadership if they knew that repeated major violations could destroy the firm. Critics often argue that dissolving a corporation would unfairly harm innocent employees, shareholders, suppliers, and communities. That concern is real, but it is not decisive. First, corporate crime already harms innocent people—workers exposed to danger, consumers defrauded, neighborhoods polluted, patients injured, and markets distorted. A system that prioritizes the continued existence of a criminal corporation over the rights of its victims has its moral priorities backward. Second, dissolution need not mean chaotic destruction. It can be structured: assets can be sold, viable divisions transferred, workers given priority in reemployment or severance, pension obligations protected, and essential services continued under receivership or successor entities. The goal is not indiscriminate economic wreckage; it is to end the legal life of an organization that has proven itself unworthy of operating.
